detailed_rationale:
Techno Electric & Engineering Company Ltd is a power-infrastructure EPC player (EPC is ~99% of FY25 revenue) executing projects across 17 Indian locations, with asset-ownership and O&M activities alongside its core construction business. On the surface the numbers look genuinely strong: five-year sales and profit CAGRs of 30% and 25% respectively, TTM sales growth of 43%, ROE of 12.2% and ROCE of 14.8%, an almost debt-free balance sheet (Rs 72 crore borrowings versus Rs 4,134 crore of reserves), and a P/E of 25.9x that does not look demanding against that growth rate.

The item that overrides all of that for me is working capital: days of working capital jumped from 92 in FY25 to 430 in FY26 -- roughly a 4.7x deterioration in a single year. Even allowing for the well-known fact that EPC contractors serving state transmission utilities and discoms face chronically slow-paying government counterparties, a jump of this magnitude in one year is well outside 'normal slow government payment' territory and typically signals either a large build-up of unbilled/contract-asset revenue (a percentage-of-completion accounting effect that can be legitimate but also a way for revenue recognition to run ahead of actual cash collection) or genuine collection stress with specific discom customers, several of which are known to be under real financial strain. I could not confirm from public sources which of these explanations applies, and I am not willing to assume the more benign one without evidence.

Reverse-DCF: 25.9x earnings for 30-43% growth and 12-15% ROE would ordinarily look like a reasonably priced growth compounder, and if the working-capital swing turns out to be a one-off accounting/timing effect tied to specific large annuity projects, this name could well be undervalued. But given the scale of the deterioration and my inability to verify its cause, I think the more disciplined call for an existing-holdings review is to treat this as an open earnings-quality question rather than credit the headline growth and margin numbers at face value.
recommendation_rationale: Growth (30-43%), returns (12.2% ROE / 14.8% ROCE) and balance-sheet leverage (near debt-free) all look genuinely strong, and the valuation (25.9x) is not demanding for that profile. However, working-capital days jumped nearly 5x in a single year (92 to 430), an unexplained anomaly of a scale I am not comfortable waving through as ordinary government-client slow-pay. Given I could not verify the cause, I am keeping this at Sell rather than rescuing it, pending clarity on what is driving the collection/unbilled-revenue build-up.
summary: Techno Electric is a power-infrastructure construction company with strong reported growth, healthy returns on capital, and almost no debt, at a valuation that isn't demanding for that growth rate. However, the time it takes the company to collect cash after billing has stretched dramatically over the past year, a red flag we could not fully explain from public information. Given that unresolved concern, we rate this a Sell for now.
positive_para: Reported growth is strong and consistent (30% five-year sales CAGR, 43% TTM), return ratios are solid (12.2% ROE, 14.8% ROCE), the balance sheet carries almost no debt, and the 25.9x earnings multiple is not demanding relative to that growth -- on the numbers that are clearly disclosed, this looks like a genuine infrastructure-growth compounder.
negative_para: Working-capital days ballooned from 92 to 430 over the last year, a nearly five-fold deterioration in cash-collection efficiency that is unusual even by the standards of EPC companies serving slow-paying government and discom clients. Without a clear explanation -- whether it is a legitimate unbilled-revenue build on large annuity projects or genuine collection stress with specific customers -- this is exactly the kind of earnings-quality question that should give an existing holder pause despite otherwise-strong reported growth and margins.
reverse_dcf_judgment: At 25.9x earnings, 30-43% growth and 12-15% ROE would normally look reasonably priced, even attractive. But the working-capital cycle blew out almost 5x in a single year, and I could not verify from available sources whether that reflects benign project-timing effects or real collection stress. Until that is resolved, I am not willing to credit the headline growth/return numbers at face value for valuation purposes.
